sentences.text: The C2PA Conformance Program is the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity's program of assurance "that products adhere to the Content Credentials specification, and fulfill a set of security requirements to ensure they are producing and validating C2PA data correctly" (c2pa.org/conformance); its own document defines it as "A risk-based governance program" whose processes, policies and requirements designate generator and validator products as conforming products and certification authorities as adhering to the C2PA Certificate Policy (C2PA Conformance Program v0.2, §2.11), and the provenance census records it, with its Explorer, as a registry of the media lineage that expresses and records provenance (provenance census record).

The conformance page calls it "a risk-based, transparent and unbiased governance process" holding generator products, validator products and certification authorities accountable to the specification, the Certificate Policy and the Security Requirements (c2pa.org/conformance), the Content Authenticity Initiative's documentation lists the same three roles (CAI open-source docs), and Andy Parsons of the CAI likens it to the Bluetooth and Wi-Fi programs, "baseline assurance for content provenance" that validates an implementation "correctly creates, signs, and reads C2PA manifests" (CAI blog, 9 October 2025); the program document says why it exists: the specification "is limited without a robust governance framework and conformance program" giving relying parties transparency and governed parties accountability (v0.2, §1).

It is part of a C2PA Governance Framework governed by the C2PA Steering Committee and administered by the C2PA Conformance Task Force (c2pa.org/conformance), a task force established in early-to-mid 2024 on the Trust over IP Governance Metamodel (Wikipedia, Content Credentials) and co-chaired by Parsons, Yogesh Deshpande (Arm) and Sherif Hanna (Google) (CAI blog); the program document has it "administered by an independent Administrator who is free from conflicts of interest" (v0.2, §6.6.3), and the census records its operator as the C2PA's Conformance Task Force, dependent on the Steering Committee, the Trust List, the TSA Trust List and the Certificate Policy (provenance census record); the coalition itself has no Wikipedia article of its own, its names redirecting to a section of the Content Authenticity Initiative article that gives it as "an open, cross-industry technical standards body established on February 22, 2021" (Wikipedia).

Its unit is the listed product: "Conforming products are placed on a publicly-accessible list," which the operator says conveys confidence and "guarantees interoperability" (c2pa.org/conformance); the C2PA Conforming Products List is "The canonical record of all Conforming Products," and because the generator product "is always the Signer" and always the listed entity, it is accountable for the conformance of the assets it generates (v0.2, §2.12, §2.26); the census gives the unit as "a conforming generator or validator product, or a trust-list entry" and the provenance object as a digital asset with its Content Credential, where "the registry's own unit is the product or signer" (provenance census record).

Acceptance adds a product to the list, which "indicates it is compliant," and a conforming validator "produces correct validation results" (CAI open-source docs); the FAQ says listed products are "vetted by the Administering Authority," "providing visibility into which implementations are trusted," and that content signed by them can be expected to carry "a higher level of implementation trust" (C2PA FAQ); SSL.com says a listing "signals to the broader ecosystem that your implementation is trustworthy, interoperable, and secure" (SSL.com, 16 July 2026); and the C2PA reserves the right to remove applicants from the trust lists or revoke conformant status (v0.2, §6.7.3).

The program governs a chain of signing: "Only instances of conforming Generator Products are eligible to receive C2PA Claim Signing Certificates from a Certification Authority on the C2PA Trust List" (v0.2, §2.23); the Trust List is "a curated list of Certification Authorities" authorised to issue signing certificates only to products the program approved (C2PA FAQ); CAs that meet the certificate policy can be on it, and a conforming generator signs a claim "using a valid X.509 certificate on the C2PA trust list" (CAI open-source docs); CAs on it, SSL.com among them, "can only issue production-grade Claim Signing Certificates to conforming products" (SSL.com).

The census names the relations the chain carries as signing, creation and edit history (ingredients) and trust-list membership, and its carrier as "signed C2PA manifests; the conformance lists as JSON" (provenance census record); Parsons calls the standard, the tools, the conformance process and the trust model together "a unified system for establishing digital provenance at scale" (CAI blog).

#1443 reads the trust model the program governs from C2PA's own literature: trust "extended to many entities by assumption and opt-in," "validation is not required by the specification," coverage of the whole file not required, and "trusted does not necessarily imply trustworthy"; "C2PA attests what a device reports having done," which "requires trusting a chain of signers," where a content-derived identifier requires trusting SHA-256 (#1443, §6.1).

#1443 holds the two "complementary rather than competing," a C2PA-signed capture that is also content-addressed and publicly witnessed being "better evidenced than either alone," and calls P.Sapph.Obbink "the human C2PA": "trust extended by assumption to a chain of signers one link deep; validation optional and unperformed" (#1443, §6.1); #1409 sets the anchors side by side, C2PA "in device and issuer certificates," the AXN regime "in content derivation plus an archive's public ledger" (#1409).

#1444 adds that C2PA is "structurally dependent on certificate authorities and platform adoption," its "trust chains revocable by exactly the class of actor that issues terminations" (#1444), the power of removal and revocation the program document reserves to the C2PA (v0.2, §6.7.3).

Two assurance levels are in operation: a product's level "indicates the level of confidence that claims it signs reflect its intended behavior," an instance's certificate may carry a level below the product's maximum (CAI open-source docs), and relying parties "are advised to review and understand the implications" of a level (v0.2, §5); Level 2 "demands more rigorous security controls, including hardware-backed key storage and dynamic security evidence," while SSL.com's rule of thumb names level 1 for devices and "at least level 1" for cloud services (SSL.com); Google's Pixel 10 was the first device at the highest level (CAI blog), and the list's first record, Google's Pixel Camera, carries maximum level 2 by Android key attestation (Conforming Products List).

Applicants sign a legal agreement with the C2PA, provide evidence and work with the program's staff (CAI open-source docs); the technical evaluation checks that manifests are properly formatted and certificates handled per the Certificate Policy, and a Conformance Letter makes the product eligible for a production claim-signing certificate from SSL.com or any approved CA on the Trust List (SSL.com).

The program was soft-launched in June 2025 at the Content Authenticity Summit at Cornell Tech and was "fully up and running" by October 2025 (CAI blog), Wikipedia giving 4 June 2025, a full public launch in October 2025 and the Interim Trust List deprecated on 31 December 2025 (Wikipedia, Content Credentials); its version table runs v0.1 from 2025-06-02 to its sunset on 2026-10-09, supporting specification v2.2, and v0.2 from 2026-07-31, sunset not set, supporting v2.2 and v2.4 (v0.2, Table 1), the document dated "Version 0.2, 2026-07-31" (v0.2, title page) and announced the same day on LinkedIn (Scott Perry, title and snippet only); the conformance page says it opened in June 2025 and is now v0.2 (c2pa.org/conformance), and the census records it active, "program opened June 2025, now v0.2," read as program v0.2 and Explainer 2.4 on 2026-10-29 (provenance census record).

The Conformance Explorer is the program's "human-readable form of our public trust lists" (v0.2, §6.6.8), where one may "Browse, search, and filter the live versions" of the Conforming Products List, the Trust List and the TSA Trust List, each product record giving its program version, maximum assurance level and supported media (Conformance Explorer); the census gives access as "Conformance Explorer; JSON lists on GitHub" (provenance census record).

The JSON list held 286 records when the census read it (provenance census record; Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), every record conformant, 254 of them generator and 32 validator products, 11 generator products at maximum level 2 (Conforming Products List); Wikipedia's section says the Explorer indexes "over 200 active products" while 10 organizations have deployed products that both complete the program and are on the Trust List (Wikipedia, Content Credentials).

What a conforming product signs is a Content Credential: provenance, "as C2PA defines it," is "the facts about the history of a piece of digital content," and the Content Credential is "a cryptographically bound structure that records an asset’s provenance" (Explainer 2.4); the FAQ gives "tamper-evident, cryptographically signed data structures that travel with the asset" and says they are "not a form of DRM" (C2PA FAQ).

In the archive's reading this is the artifact dimension of provenance: artifact provenance "verifies that *this file* was created by *this source* at *this time*," necessary and operating "at the moment of artifact creation" (#725, §1.4), C2PA / Content Credentials being the "Cryptographic signing of content creation events" (#725, §4); "C2PA tells you whether the artifact's signing event was real" (#725, §11), "C2PA verifies file history" (#729), and it answers "is this real?" (#50); #127 says the manifest "records authorship, edits, tool chain, and AI involvement" (#127).

C2PA states the governing limit itself: Content Credentials "do not provide value judgments about whether a given set of provenance data is 'true'," only whether it is well-formed, untampered, valid and trusted, trusted in that "the signer of the Content Credential is associated with a known trust list," and "provenance information alone cannot tell you whether the digital content is true, accurate or factual" (Explainer 2.4); the census carries this as its first negative tag (provenance census record), the Wikipedia article as the distinction that "a fabricated or misleading image can maintain a valid cryptographic credential" (Wikipedia, Content Credentials), and the criticism that signing tools do not verify the accuracy of the metadata either (Wikipedia, Content Authenticity Initiative).

#725 gives the mechanism with a case it attributes to Hacker Factor: "cryptographically valid C2PA signatures can be applied to forged or AI-generated content," the signature verifying the signing event "but does not verify the truth of what is signed," which it calls "not a flaw of C2PA" but "a structural property of *all* signature-based systems" (#725, §3.6); #1443 says C2PA cannot "establish the truth of depicted content" (#1443, §6.1).

On identity and authorship the sources state one limit at different grains: the core specification "does not support attribution of content to individuals or organizations" (C2PA FAQ) and "does not directly address the topic of human or organizational identity" (Explainer 2.4; the census's third negative tag, provenance census record); accreditation "enables users to trust in that implementation," while trust in a credential's contents rests on the relationship of its creator and its consumer, which "is not defined by the C2PA" (Explainer 2.4); #729 reads it as "C2PA prevents forgery; it does not constitute authorship," the signature telling "what tool made it" and not whether the human who used the tool is accountable (#729), and #1444 as securing "the camera's testimony, not the author's" (#1444).

Two archive statements stand against the FAQ's limit and are composed beside it: #127 has the manifest record "authorship" (#127), and #1003 groups C2PA among provenance and attribution studies that "have focused on attribution loss in AI outputs" (#1003); #784 reads the register in which "Concerns that would be named *meaning* and *attribution* are governed here as *content authenticity* and *information integrity*" (#784).

The chain of provenance is not whole: "Provenance is not always complete," the metadata "can be removed" (Explainer 2.4), and manifests "can be separated," soft bindings helping to rediscover them (C2PA FAQ); an ingredient's provenance "cannot be verified in the same way" as the containing asset's (Explainer 2.4; carried by the census as evidence, provenance census record), so that without its data "only the presence of prior validation" is confirmed (C2PA FAQ); #725 adds that ingredient assertions are "optional, under-adopted," operating "at the level of file derivation, not concept lineage" (#725).

The program bounds itself: of "over 300 normative requirements" on generator products it "will eventually require" complete conformance (v0.2, §6.1.1), and the census records that it tests no transformation, "not tested here: conformance concerns producing and validating C2PA data correctly," leaving the trust-list entries and "the latest specification version" unchecked (provenance census record).

On security the sources conflict: the FAQ says tampering makes "alterations immediately detectable" and that faking credentials "would require breaking current cryptographic standards" (C2PA FAQ); Wikipedia reports that in October 2026 David Buchanan demonstrated a vulnerability allowing an image to be altered "without invalidating its cryptographic signatures or trusted timestamps," and that in August 2026 on Android root access let the system sign fabricated images "with valid authenticity signatures," which Google marked "Won't fix (infeasible)" (Wikipedia, Content Credentials), and the Content Authenticity Initiative article cites documented ways in which "attackers can bypass C2PA’s safeguards" (Wikipedia, Content Authenticity Initiative).

Adoption is partial: as of 2026 no dedicated camera and as of mid-2026 no desktop application had achieved compliance, Leica, Nikon and Canon standing outside the program (Wikipedia, Content Credentials); #725 found adoption "uneven," verification interfaces "nascent" and "the social infrastructure of trust" still being built (#725), #499 that C2PA had not "achieved sufficient adoption to function as infrastructure" (#499, February 2026), and the census's neighbour IPTC Metawatch found 27 C2PA manifests in 6,580 news images in October 2026 (provenance census record).

#725 places what the program certifies among the dimensions of provenance: existing frameworks "address the artifact (C2PA / Content Credentials) and the corpus" and "are not designed to address the survival of authorial lineage through AI synthesis"; the dimensions are independent, "a C2PA-signed image can carry meaning whose lineage has been eroded"; its relation to C2PA is "Extension and completion, not substitution or critique" (#725); and #729 and #1386 add process provenance as a third dimension beside artifact provenance, which #729 marks "Necessary, insufficient" (#729; #1386).

Past the artifact the archive finds no reach: a signed image whose caption a model rewrites without the photographer's name "has lost semantic provenance even though artifact provenance is preserved" (#725, §3.1); "When a 5,000-word article becomes a 200-word AI Overview, C2PA cannot tell you what was lost" (#615); for text on the open web it "has no operational analogue that survives" (#127); it "Doesn't cover text, doesn't handle multi-step AI generation" (#621); it does not address the reception consequences of provenance, attribution and disambiguation (#833); and it is a starting point for the public and machine-readable layers of attribution only (#95).

The archive meets the trust chain at its own artifacts: only conforming products receive certificates from Trust List CAs (SSL.com), and Google surfaces C2PA manifests "(≥v2.1, Trust List CA)" in About This Image (#1409); #1409 grades its handwritten artifacts self-signed, verifiable but not surfaced, as the floor, and Trust-List-signed, "eligible for About This Image surfacing," where the toolchain permits, leaving open which toolchain is acceptable (#1409); earlier it listed C2PA as a standard its own provenance document complies with by serving "as machine-readable provenance data" (#208), planned a "C2PA-compatible" manifest layer (#204), and set its Non-Mutual Extraction Notice in the genre of "C2PA provenance signals," honoured "by reading, not by enforcement" (#914).

The census asks of the program "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?" and tags it "NOT IPTC embedded metadata" (provenance census record); at the name on Google's AI Overview on 2026-10-29 the composition "says what the program certifies, who takes part, how a product is admitted and why admission matters for signing," the program "composed as its applicants meet it: components and steps," its purpose the conformance page's ("producing and validating C2PA data correctly"), the products list its unit, v0.2 through the LinkedIn card, and the registry attributes "'Risk-based governance'" to Trufo's card (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), where the card is the C2PA's own program document, whose glossary opens "A risk-based governance program" (v0.2, §2.11), and the conformance page has "a risk-based, transparent and unbiased governance process" (c2pa.org/conformance).

The registry records the limit left out: the record's negative tags "are C2PA's own" (Explainer 2.4), the composition gives "'end-to-end tamper evidence for digital media'" and omits them, "the half of the record that bears on provenance, does not reach the composition," and "A reader leaves with tamper evidence and without the caveat that well-formed provenance can be false"; the census record landed the same day "and no card cites it" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

P.title: C2PA Conformance Program

lede.text: is the C2PA's program for Content Credentials products: generators, validators and certification authorities that conform go on public lists, and only conforming generators get signing certificates from Trust List CAs. It certifies correct production and validation of signed provenance, not its truth: C2PA's own Explainer says Content Credentials make no judgement of whether provenance is "true" (c2pa.org/conformance; v0.2; Explainer 2.4; #725; provenance census record).

items.label: Governance:
items.text: a risk-based program of the C2PA Steering Committee, run by its Conformance Task Force (2024) through an independent Administrator.

items.label: The unit:
items.text: the listed product; the generator product is always the signer (v0.2; census).

items.label: Versions:
items.text: opened June 2025; v0.1 sunset 9 Oct 2026; v0.2 since 31 Jul 2026 (Table 1).

items.label: Certificates:
items.text: Trust List CAs issue claim-signing certificates only to conforming generators (v0.2; FAQ; SSL.com).

items.label: Levels:
items.text: 1 and 2; level 2 needs hardware-backed keys; Pixel first at level 2. Entry: agreement, evidence, Conformance Letter.

items.label: Trust model:
items.text: trust by assumption to a chain of signers, "trusted does not necessarily imply trustworthy" (#1443); chains revocable by those who issue terminations (#1444).

items.label: The list:
items.text: 286 conformant records, 254 generators (Explorer; census; JSON).

items.label: Truth:
items.text: valid signatures can sit on forged or AI-made content, a property of all signature systems (#725; Wikipedia).

items.label: Authorship:
items.text: no attribution or identity in the core spec (FAQ; Explainer); "C2PA prevents forgery; it does not constitute authorship" (#729). #127 and #1003 say otherwise.

items.label: Whole chains:
items.text: provenance can be incomplete, removed or separated; ingredients unverifiable (Explainer; FAQ).

items.label: Full conformance:
items.text: "will eventually" be required (v0.2); no survival tested (census).

items.label: Security:
items.text: the FAQ calls forgery infeasible; 2026 demonstrations altered and forged signed images (Wikipedia).

items.label: Dimensions:
items.text: the artifact layer; lineage through AI synthesis is another dimension (#725, #729, #1386).

items.label: Reach:
items.text: no text analogue; cannot say what an AI Overview lost (#127, #615, #621).

items.label: Adoption:
items.text: no conformant dedicated camera (Wikipedia); 27 manifests in 6,580 news images (census).

items.label: The archive:
items.text: grades its artifacts self-signed or Trust-List-signed (#1409).

items.label: Here:
items.text: the Overview gave tamper evidence and dropped the limit (Capture Registry).

sentences.text: The C2PA Conformance Program gives assurance that products adhere to the Content Credentials specification and meet security requirements, producing and validating C2PA data correctly; it is a risk-based governance program designating generator and validator products as conforming and certification authorities as adhering to the Certificate Policy (c2pa.org/conformance; program document v0.2).

It sits in the C2PA Governance Framework under the Steering Committee and is administered by the Conformance Task Force, set up in 2024 and co-chaired from the CAI, Arm and Google, through an independent Administrator (c2pa.org/conformance; Wikipedia; CAI blog; v0.2); the coalition, founded in 2021, has no article of its own on Wikipedia (Wikipedia).

Conforming products go on a public list, the canonical Conforming Products List, where the generator product is always the signer and accountable for its assets, and the FAQ and SSL.com read a listing as visibility of trusted, interoperable and secure implementations, subject to removal or revocation (c2pa.org/conformance; v0.2; CAI docs; C2PA FAQ; SSL.com).

Only conforming generator products may receive claim-signing certificates from CAs on the curated C2PA Trust List, signing claims with X.509 certificates, in what the CAI calls a unified system of standard, tools, conformance and trust model (v0.2; C2PA FAQ; CAI docs; SSL.com; CAI blog).

There are two assurance levels, level 2 requiring hardware-backed keys and dynamic evidence, an instance's level possibly below the product's maximum; Google's Pixel 10 was first at the highest level (CAI docs; v0.2; SSL.com; CAI blog; Conforming Products List).
Applicants sign a legal agreement, provide evidence, pass a technical evaluation and receive a Conformance Letter before a production certificate (CAI docs; SSL.com).

It soft-launched in June 2025 and launched fully in October 2025; v0.1 ran from 2 June 2025 to 9 October 2026 and v0.2 began on 31 July 2026, supporting specifications 2.2 and 2.4 (CAI blog; Wikipedia; v0.2; Scott Perry; c2pa.org/conformance).

The Conformance Explorer browses the live Conforming Products List, Trust List and TSA Trust List; the list held 286 conformant records, against Wikipedia's count of over 200 products and 10 organizations both conforming and on the Trust List (v0.2; Conformance Explorer; Conforming Products List; Wikipedia).
What is signed is a Content Credential, a cryptographically bound, tamper-evident structure recording an asset's provenance, not DRM (Explainer 2.4; C2PA FAQ).

Content Credentials do not judge whether provenance is true, only whether it is well-formed, untampered, valid and trusted; the core specification does not support attribution or address identity; provenance can be incomplete, removed or separated, and ingredients cannot be fully verified (Explainer 2.4; C2PA FAQ; Wikipedia).
The program will only eventually require complete conformance to the specification's normative requirements (v0.2).

The FAQ calls faking credentials infeasible, while Wikipedia reports demonstrated breaks in 2026 and criticism of bypasses; no dedicated camera or desktop application had achieved compliance (C2PA FAQ; Wikipedia).

L_BA.text: The C2PA Conformance Program is the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity's program of assurance "that products adhere to the Content Credentials specification, and fulfill a set of security requirements to ensure they are producing and validating C2PA data correctly" (c2pa.org/conformance); its own document defines it as "A risk-based governance program" whose processes, policies and requirements designate generator and validator products as conforming products and certification authorities as adhering to the C2PA Certificate Policy (C2PA Conformance Program v0.2, §2.11), and the provenance census records it, with its Explorer, as a registry of the media lineage that expresses and records provenance (provenance census record). The conformance page calls it "a risk-based, transparent and unbiased governance process" holding generator products, validator products and certification authorities accountable to the specification, the Certificate Policy and the Security Requirements (c2pa.org/conformance), the Content Authenticity Initiative's documentation lists the same three roles (CAI open-source docs), and Andy Parsons of the CAI likens it to the Bluetooth and Wi-Fi programs, "baseline assurance for content provenance" that validates an implementation "correctly creates, signs, and reads C2PA manifests" (CAI blog, 9 October 2025); the program document says why it exists: the specification "is limited without a robust governance framework and conformance program" giving relying parties transparency and governed parties accountability (v0.2, §1). It is part of a C2PA Governance Framework governed by the C2PA Steering Committee and administered by the C2PA Conformance Task Force (c2pa.org/conformance), a task force established in early-to-mid 2024 on the Trust over IP Governance Metamodel (Wikipedia, Content Credentials) and co-chaired by Parsons, Yogesh Deshpande (Arm) and Sherif Hanna (Google) (CAI blog); the program document has it "administered by an independent Administrator who is free from conflicts of interest" (v0.2, §6.6.3), and the census records its operator as the C2PA's Conformance Task Force, dependent on the Steering Committee, the Trust List, the TSA Trust List and the Certificate Policy (provenance census record); the coalition itself has no Wikipedia article of its own, its names redirecting to a section of the Content Authenticity Initiative article that gives it as "an open, cross-industry technical standards body established on February 22, 2021" (Wikipedia). Its unit is the listed product: "Conforming products are placed on a publicly-accessible list," which the operator says conveys confidence and "guarantees interoperability" (c2pa.org/conformance); the C2PA Conforming Products List is "The canonical record of all Conforming Products," and because the generator product "is always the Signer" and always the listed entity, it is accountable for the conformance of the assets it generates (v0.2, §2.12, §2.26); the census gives the unit as "a conforming generator or validator product, or a trust-list entry" and the provenance object as a digital asset with its Content Credential, where "the registry's own unit is the product or signer" (provenance census record). Acceptance adds a product to the list, which "indicates it is compliant," and a conforming validator "produces correct validation results" (CAI open-source docs); the FAQ says listed products are "vetted by the Administering Authority," "providing visibility into which implementations are trusted," and that content signed by them can be expected to carry "a higher level of implementation trust" (C2PA FAQ); SSL.com says a listing "signals to the broader ecosystem that your implementation is trustworthy, interoperable, and secure" (SSL.com, 16 July 2026); and the C2PA reserves the right to remove applicants from the trust lists or revoke conformant status (v0.2, §6.7.3). The program governs a chain of signing: "Only instances of conforming Generator Products are eligible to receive C2PA Claim Signing Certificates from a Certification Authority on the C2PA Trust List" (v0.2, §2.23); the Trust List is "a curated list of Certification Authorities" authorised to issue signing certificates only to products the program approved (C2PA FAQ); CAs that meet the certificate policy can be on it, and a conforming generator signs a claim "using a valid X.509 certificate on the C2PA trust list" (CAI open-source docs); CAs on it, SSL.com among them, "can only issue production-grade Claim Signing Certificates to conforming products" (SSL.com). The census names the relations the chain carries as signing, creation and edit history (ingredients) and trust-list membership, and its carrier as "signed C2PA manifests; the conformance lists as JSON" (provenance census record); Parsons calls the standard, the tools, the conformance process and the trust model together "a unified system for establishing digital provenance at scale" (CAI blog). #1443 reads the trust model the program governs from C2PA's own literature: trust "extended to many entities by assumption and opt-in," "validation is not required by the specification," coverage of the whole file not required, and "trusted does not necessarily imply trustworthy"; "C2PA attests what a device reports having done," which "requires trusting a chain of signers," where a content-derived identifier requires trusting SHA-256 (#1443, §6.1). #1443 holds the two "complementary rather than competing," a C2PA-signed capture that is also content-addressed and publicly witnessed being "better evidenced than either alone," and calls P.Sapph.Obbink "the human C2PA": "trust extended by assumption to a chain of signers one link deep; validation optional and unperformed" (#1443, §6.1); #1409 sets the anchors side by side, C2PA "in device and issuer certificates," the AXN regime "in content derivation plus an archive's public ledger" (#1409). #1444 adds that C2PA is "structurally dependent on certificate authorities and platform adoption," its "trust chains revocable by exactly the class of actor that issues terminations" (#1444), the power of removal and revocation the program document reserves to the C2PA (v0.2, §6.7.3). Two assurance levels are in operation: a product's level "indicates the level of confidence that claims it signs reflect its intended behavior," an instance's certificate may carry a level below the product's maximum (CAI open-source docs), and relying parties "are advised to review and understand the implications" of a level (v0.2, §5); Level 2 "demands more rigorous security controls, including hardware-backed key storage and dynamic security evidence," while SSL.com's rule of thumb names level 1 for devices and "at least level 1" for cloud services (SSL.com); Google's Pixel 10 was the first device at the highest level (CAI blog), and the list's first record, Google's Pixel Camera, carries maximum level 2 by Android key attestation (Conforming Products List). Applicants sign a legal agreement with the C2PA, provide evidence and work with the program's staff (CAI open-source docs); the technical evaluation checks that manifests are properly formatted and certificates handled per the Certificate Policy, and a Conformance Letter makes the product eligible for a production claim-signing certificate from SSL.com or any approved CA on the Trust List (SSL.com). The program was soft-launched in June 2025 at the Content Authenticity Summit at Cornell Tech and was "fully up and running" by October 2025 (CAI blog), Wikipedia giving 4 June 2025, a full public launch in October 2025 and the Interim Trust List deprecated on 31 December 2025 (Wikipedia, Content Credentials); its version table runs v0.1 from 2025-06-02 to its sunset on 2026-10-09, supporting specification v2.2, and v0.2 from 2026-07-31, sunset not set, supporting v2.2 and v2.4 (v0.2, Table 1), the document dated "Version 0.2, 2026-07-31" (v0.2, title page) and announced the same day on LinkedIn (Scott Perry, title and snippet only); the conformance page says it opened in June 2025 and is now v0.2 (c2pa.org/conformance), and the census records it active, "program opened June 2025, now v0.2," read as program v0.2 and Explainer 2.4 on 2026-10-29 (provenance census record). The Conformance Explorer is the program's "human-readable form of our public trust lists" (v0.2, §6.6.8), where one may "Browse, search, and filter the live versions" of the Conforming Products List, the Trust List and the TSA Trust List, each product record giving its program version, maximum assurance level and supported media (Conformance Explorer); the census gives access as "Conformance Explorer; JSON lists on GitHub" (provenance census record). The JSON list held 286 records when the census read it (provenance census record; Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), every record conformant, 254 of them generator and 32 validator products, 11 generator products at maximum level 2 (Conforming Products List); Wikipedia's section says the Explorer indexes "over 200 active products" while 10 organizations have deployed products that both complete the program and are on the Trust List (Wikipedia, Content Credentials). What a conforming product signs is a Content Credential: provenance, "as C2PA defines it," is "the facts about the history of a piece of digital content," and the Content Credential is "a cryptographically bound structure that records an asset’s provenance" (Explainer 2.4); the FAQ gives "tamper-evident, cryptographically signed data structures that travel with the asset" and says they are "not a form of DRM" (C2PA FAQ). In the archive's reading this is the artifact dimension of provenance: artifact provenance "verifies that *this file* was created by *this source* at *this time*," necessary and operating "at the moment of artifact creation" (#725, §1.4), C2PA / Content Credentials being the "Cryptographic signing of content creation events" (#725, §4); "C2PA tells you whether the artifact's signing event was real" (#725, §11), "C2PA verifies file history" (#729), and it answers "is this real?" (#50); #127 says the manifest "records authorship, edits, tool chain, and AI involvement" (#127). C2PA states the governing limit itself: Content Credentials "do not provide value judgments about whether a given set of provenance data is 'true'," only whether it is well-formed, untampered, valid and trusted, trusted in that "the signer of the Content Credential is associated with a known trust list," and "provenance information alone cannot tell you whether the digital content is true, accurate or factual" (Explainer 2.4); the census carries this as its first negative tag (provenance census record), the Wikipedia article as the distinction that "a fabricated or misleading image can maintain a valid cryptographic credential" (Wikipedia, Content Credentials), and the criticism that signing tools do not verify the accuracy of the metadata either (Wikipedia, Content Authenticity Initiative). #725 gives the mechanism with a case it attributes to Hacker Factor: "cryptographically valid C2PA signatures can be applied to forged or AI-generated content," the signature verifying the signing event "but does not verify the truth of what is signed," which it calls "not a flaw of C2PA" but "a structural property of *all* signature-based systems" (#725, §3.6); #1443 says C2PA cannot "establish the truth of depicted content" (#1443, §6.1). On identity and authorship the sources state one limit at different grains: the core specification "does not support attribution of content to individuals or organizations" (C2PA FAQ) and "does not directly address the topic of human or organizational identity" (Explainer 2.4; the census's third negative tag, provenance census record); accreditation "enables users to trust in that implementation," while trust in a credential's contents rests on the relationship of its creator and its consumer, which "is not defined by the C2PA" (Explainer 2.4); #729 reads it as "C2PA prevents forgery; it does not constitute authorship," the signature telling "what tool made it" and not whether the human who used the tool is accountable (#729), and #1444 as securing "the camera's testimony, not the author's" (#1444). Two archive statements stand against the FAQ's limit and are composed beside it: #127 has the manifest record "authorship" (#127), and #1003 groups C2PA among provenance and attribution studies that "have focused on attribution loss in AI outputs" (#1003); #784 reads the register in which "Concerns that would be named *meaning* and *attribution* are governed here as *content authenticity* and *information integrity*" (#784). The chain of provenance is not whole: "Provenance is not always complete," the metadata "can be removed" (Explainer 2.4), and manifests "can be separated," soft bindings helping to rediscover them (C2PA FAQ); an ingredient's provenance "cannot be verified in the same way" as the containing asset's (Explainer 2.4; carried by the census as evidence, provenance census record), so that without its data "only the presence of prior validation" is confirmed (C2PA FAQ); #725 adds that ingredient assertions are "optional, under-adopted," operating "at the level of file derivation, not concept lineage" (#725). The program bounds itself: of "over 300 normative requirements" on generator products it "will eventually require" complete conformance (v0.2, §6.1.1), and the census records that it tests no transformation, "not tested here: conformance concerns producing and validating C2PA data correctly," leaving the trust-list entries and "the latest specification version" unchecked (provenance census record). On security the sources conflict: the FAQ says tampering makes "alterations immediately detectable" and that faking credentials "would require breaking current cryptographic standards" (C2PA FAQ); Wikipedia reports that in October 2026 David Buchanan demonstrated a vulnerability allowing an image to be altered "without invalidating its cryptographic signatures or trusted timestamps," and that in August 2026 on Android root access let the system sign fabricated images "with valid authenticity signatures," which Google marked "Won't fix (infeasible)" (Wikipedia, Content Credentials), and the Content Authenticity Initiative article cites documented ways in which "attackers can bypass C2PA’s safeguards" (Wikipedia, Content Authenticity Initiative). Adoption is partial: as of 2026 no dedicated camera and as of mid-2026 no desktop application had achieved compliance, Leica, Nikon and Canon standing outside the program (Wikipedia, Content Credentials); #725 found adoption "uneven," verification interfaces "nascent" and "the social infrastructure of trust" still being built (#725), #499 that C2PA had not "achieved sufficient adoption to function as infrastructure" (#499, February 2026), and the census's neighbour IPTC Metawatch found 27 C2PA manifests in 6,580 news images in October 2026 (provenance census record). #725 places what the program certifies among the dimensions of provenance: existing frameworks "address the artifact (C2PA / Content Credentials) and the corpus" and "are not designed to address the survival of authorial lineage through AI synthesis"; the dimensions are independent, "a C2PA-signed image can carry meaning whose lineage has been eroded"; its relation to C2PA is "Extension and completion, not substitution or critique" (#725); and #729 and #1386 add process provenance as a third dimension beside artifact provenance, which #729 marks "Necessary, insufficient" (#729; #1386). Past the artifact the archive finds no reach: a signed image whose caption a model rewrites without the photographer's name "has lost semantic provenance even though artifact provenance is preserved" (#725, §3.1); "When a 5,000-word article becomes a 200-word AI Overview, C2PA cannot tell you what was lost" (#615); for text on the open web it "has no operational analogue that survives" (#127); it "Doesn't cover text, doesn't handle multi-step AI generation" (#621); it does not address the reception consequences of provenance, attribution and disambiguation (#833); and it is a starting point for the public and machine-readable layers of attribution only (#95). The archive meets the trust chain at its own artifacts: only conforming products receive certificates from Trust List CAs (SSL.com), and Google surfaces C2PA manifests "(≥v2.1, Trust List CA)" in About This Image (#1409); #1409 grades its handwritten artifacts self-signed, verifiable but not surfaced, as the floor, and Trust-List-signed, "eligible for About This Image surfacing," where the toolchain permits, leaving open which toolchain is acceptable (#1409); earlier it listed C2PA as a standard its own provenance document complies with by serving "as machine-readable provenance data" (#208), planned a "C2PA-compatible" manifest layer (#204), and set its Non-Mutual Extraction Notice in the genre of "C2PA provenance signals," honoured "by reading, not by enforcement" (#914). The census asks of the program "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?" and tags it "NOT IPTC embedded metadata" (provenance census record); at the name on Google's AI Overview on 2026-10-29 the composition "says what the program certifies, who takes part, how a product is admitted and why admission matters for signing," the program "composed as its applicants meet it: components and steps," its purpose the conformance page's ("producing and validating C2PA data correctly"), the products list its unit, v0.2 through the LinkedIn card, and the registry attributes "'Risk-based governance'" to Trufo's card (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), where the card is the C2PA's own program document, whose glossary opens "A risk-based governance program" (v0.2, §2.11), and the conformance page has "a risk-based, transparent and unbiased governance process" (c2pa.org/conformance). The registry records the limit left out: the record's negative tags "are C2PA's own" (Explainer 2.4), the composition gives "'end-to-end tamper evidence for digital media'" and omits them, "the half of the record that bears on provenance, does not reach the composition," and "A reader leaves with tamper evidence and without the caveat that well-formed provenance can be false"; the census record landed the same day "and no card cites it" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

F12.lineage: the trust chain: only conforming generator products get claim-signing certificates

F13.quote: In June, the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) soft-launched the C2PA Conformance Program during the Content Authenticity Summit at Cornell Tech in New York City. The program is now fully up and running, accepting submissions and encouraging participation from software developers, device makers, and certification authorities.
F13.claim: soft-launched in June 2025 at the Content Authenticity Summit, Cornell Tech; fully running by October 2025
F13.lineage: origin and versions: June 2025 (v0.1) to v0.2 (31 July 2026)

F14.quote: Just as the Bluetooth® or Wi-Fi® programs verify that devices communicate reliably and securely across manufacturers, the C2PA Conformance Program provides baseline assurance for content provenance. It validates that an implementation correctly creates, signs, and reads C2PA manifests, while protecting those manifests and their associated assets through proven cryptographic methods and certificate validation.
F14.claim: baseline assurance for content provenance, on the model of Bluetooth or Wi-Fi certification: it validates that an implementation creates, signs and reads manifests correctly
F14.lineage: what it is: a conformance program for Content Credentials implementations

F15.locus: A foundation for security and interoperability ¶1
F15.quote: At launch, the program introduces two security levels, offering flexibility for a diverse set of implementers while establishing a clear path toward more rigorous, hardware-backed assurance. Notably, Google has already achieved the highest conformance level for the Pixel 10, making it the first device to meet the strongest requirements for secure provenance capture and signing.
F15.claim: two security levels at launch; Google's Pixel 10 the first device at the highest level

F16.locus: A foundation for security and interoperability ¶3
F16.quote: With the introduction of the Conformance Program, all these elements — the standard, the tools, the conformance process, and the trust model — now work together as a unified system for establishing digital provenance at scale.
F16.claim: the standard, the tools, the conformance process and the trust model as one system for digital provenance at scale
F16.lineage: the trust chain: only conforming generator products get claim-signing certificates

F17.quote: This program is the product of more than a year of dedicated collaboration within the C2PA Conformance Task Force, which I have the privilege of co-chairing alongside Yogesh Deshpande (Arm) and Sherif Hanna (Google).
F17.claim: built over more than a year in the Conformance Task Force, co-chaired by Andy Parsons (CAI), Yogesh Deshpande (Arm) and Sherif Hanna (Google)
F17.lineage: governance: the C2PA, its Steering Committee and Conformance Task Force

F18.quote: Browse, search, and filter the live versions of the C2PA Conforming Products List, C2PA Trust List, and C2PA TSA Trust List
F18.claim: the Explorer: browse, search and filter the live Conforming Products List, Trust List and TSA Trust List
F18.lineage: the Conformance Explorer and the machine-readable lists

F19.locus: Explorer (bundle UI text): product record labels
F19.quote: Conformance Program Version: Minimum Eligible Product Version: Security Assurance & Attestation Max Assurance Level: Supported Media Containers & Streams
F19.claim: each product record gives its program version, minimum product version, attestation, maximum assurance level and supported media containers
F19.lineage: the Conformance Explorer and the machine-readable lists

F20.locus: Why Is the Conformance Program Submission Necessary? ¶1
F20.quote: The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) maintains a formal conformance program to verify that generator or validator products correctly implement the Content Credentials specification. Once a product passes this requirement, it earns a spot on the publicly accessible C2PA Conforming Products List, which signals to the broader ecosystem that your implementation is trustworthy, interoperable, and secure.
F20.claim: SSL.com's account: a formal program verifying correct implementation; listing signals trustworthiness, interoperability and security
F20.lineage: the unit: conforming products on a public list, with trust lists of CAs

F21.locus: Why Is the Conformance Program Submission Necessary? ¶2
F21.quote: CAs approved for the official C2PA Trust List, including SSL, can only issue production-grade Claim Signing Certificates to conforming products. Without conformance, C2PA trusted certificates cannot be issued.
F21.claim: trust-list CAs, SSL.com among them, issue production claim-signing certificates only to conforming products
F21.lineage: the trust chain: only conforming generator products get claim-signing certificates

F22.quote: Properly formats C2PA manifests (the structured containers that hold Content Credentials and provenance data) … Handles certificates in accordance with the C2PA Certificate Policy
F22.claim: the technical evaluation: manifests formatted properly, certificates handled per the Certificate Policy
F22.lineage: the process: expression of interest, legal agreement, evidence, approval

F23.quote: The C2PA Conformance Program operates on two assurance levels. Level 1 has more flexible requirements, while Level 2 demands more rigorous security controls, including hardware-backed key storage and dynamic security evidence. Determining which level applies to your use case should be an early conversation, as it affects your implementation approach and timeline. A rule of thumb is that a C2PA implementation on a device (mobile phone, camera, cam-recorder, etc.) requires level 1, whereas a cloud service requires at least level 1.
F23.claim: Level 2 requires hardware-backed key storage and dynamic security evidence; the rule of thumb names level 1 for devices and 'at least level 1' for cloud services

F24.quote: Once the C2PA verifies your conformance and issues a Conformance Letter, you are eligible to obtain a production Claim Signing Certificate from SSL (or any approved CA on the official C2PA Trust List).
F24.claim: a Conformance Letter makes the product eligible for a production claim-signing certificate from a trust-list CA
F24.lineage: the process: expression of interest, legal agreement, evidence, approval

F25.quote: Content Credentials provide a cryptographically secure way to capture and express content provenance. … In the context of C2PA, content provenance is captured and preserved using Content Credentials, the technical standard the C2PA produces, providing tamper-evident, cryptographically signed data structures that travel with the asset.
F25.claim: Content Credentials: tamper-evident, cryptographically signed provenance data structures that travel with the asset
F25.lineage: what Content Credentials are: signed, tamper-evident provenance bound to the asset

F26.locus: FAQ: How can consumers of C2PA data be assured the data was captured correctly? ¶2
F26.quote: Additionally, the C2PA Conformance Program ensures that products creating Content Credentials meet stringent technical and security requirements and are vetted by the Administering Authority. These products are then listed in the C2PA Conforming Products List, providing visibility into which implementations are trusted.
F26.claim: the FAQ's statement of the program: products vetted by the Administering Authority and listed, giving visibility of which implementations are trusted
F26.lineage: the unit: conforming products on a public list, with trust lists of CAs

F27.locus: FAQ: Does validation … ensure that the entire chain of provenance is known, including ingredients? ¶2
F27.quote: While the primary asset’s Content Credential can validate that the ingredients were checked at the time of use, the full verification of each ingredient’s provenance requires access to its data. Without it, only the presence of prior validation (not the complete ingredient chain) can be confirmed.
F27.claim: the ingredient limit: without the ingredient's data only prior validation, not the whole chain, can be confirmed
F27.lineage: stated limits: no judgement of truth, no identity or attribution, incomplete chains

F28.locus: FAQ: Are Content Credentials a form of DRM? ¶1
F28.quote: No, Content Credentials are not a form of DRM (Digital Rights Management).
F28.lineage: what Content Credentials are: signed, tamper-evident provenance bound to the asset

F29.locus: FAQ: What happens if C2PA metadata is stripped …? ¶1
F29.quote: While C2PA Manifests are typically embedded in the asset, they can be separated. To address this, C2PA supports durable credentials via soft bindings—such as invisible watermarking or fingerprinting—that can help rediscover the associated Content Credential even if it’s removed from the file.
F29.claim: manifests can be separated from the asset; soft bindings (watermarks, fingerprints) can help rediscover them
F29.lineage: stated limits: no judgement of truth, no identity or attribution, incomplete chains

F30.locus: FAQ: What is the C2PA Trust List …? ¶1
F30.quote: The C2PA Trust List is a curated list of Certification Authorities (CAs) that are authorized to issue signing certificates for Generator Products. Only products evaluated and approved by the Conformance Program are eligible to receive certificates from these trusted CAs.
F30.claim: the Trust List: curated CAs authorised to issue signing certificates, only to products the program approved
F30.lineage: the trust chain: only conforming generator products get claim-signing certificates

F31.quote: Any tampering with the asset or its metadata invalidates the cryptographic hash and signature, making alterations immediately detectable. … Faking Content Credentials would require breaking current cryptographic standards—an infeasible task with today’s technology.
F31.claim: the FAQ's security claim: tampering is immediately detectable; faking credentials would require breaking current cryptography
F31.lineage: security: tamper evidence asserted and its demonstrated breaks
F31.mark: contested: B13 (Content Credentials § C2PA Conformance Program ¶3; Mobile apps with Camera Support) reports demonstrated alteration without invalidating signatures (October 2026) and forgery on Android (August 2026)

F32.locus: FAQ: Can organizations or individuals use Content Credentials to achieve attribution of their content? ¶1
F32.quote: The core C2PA Content Credentials specification does not support attribution of content to individuals or organizations, so that it can remain maximally privacy-preserving.
F32.claim: the core specification does not support attribution of content to individuals or organizations (for privacy)
F32.lineage: stated limits: no judgement of truth, no identity or attribution, incomplete chains

F33.locus: FAQ: What is the benefit of the new C2PA Conformance Program? ¶1
F33.quote: Consumers and validators seeing content signed by products on the Conforming Product List can expect the Program to provide them with a higher level of implementation trust.
F33.claim: the benefit claimed: a higher level of implementation trust for content signed by listed products
F33.lineage: the unit: conforming products on a public list, with trust lists of CAs

F34.quote: C2PA Conformance Program C2PA Technical Working Group Conformance Task Force Version 0.2, 2026-07-31
F34.claim: the program's own document: Version 0.2, 31 July 2026, by the Technical Working Group's Conformance Task Force
F34.lineage: origin and versions: June 2025 (v0.1) to v0.2 (31 July 2026)

F35.quote: The Specification has seen wide-scale acceptance but is limited without a robust governance framework and conformance program to provide required transparency for relying parties and accountability for governed parties which need to demonstrate recognized conformance of Specification requirements.
F35.claim: why the program exists: the specification is limited without governance and conformance providing transparency for relying parties and accountability for governed parties
F35.lineage: what it is: a conformance program for Content Credentials implementations

F36.quote: A risk-based governance program intended to hold Applicants who want to demonstrate their conformance to its requirements and then differentiate themselves through C2PA recognition by satisfying program requirements being acknowledged as achieving that level of conformance. It consists of a set of processes, policies, and requirements governing the designation of Applicant Generator Products or Validator Products as Conforming Products, and the designation of Certification Authorities as adhering to the C2PA Certificate Policy
F36.claim: the glossary definition: a risk-based governance program whose processes, policies and requirements designate generator and validator products as conforming and CAs as adhering to the Certificate Policy
F36.lineage: what it is: a conformance program for Content Credentials implementations

F37.quote: The canonical record of all Conforming Products that have been deemed conformant according to the stipulations of the C2PA Conformance Program
F37.claim: the Conforming Products List: the canonical record of all conforming products
F37.lineage: the unit: conforming products on a public list, with trust lists of CAs

F38.quote: Only instances of conforming Generator Products are eligible to receive C2PA Claim Signing Certificates from a Certification Authority on the C2PA Trust List.
F38.claim: only instances of conforming generator products may receive claim-signing certificates from a trust-list CA
F38.lineage: the trust chain: only conforming generator products get claim-signing certificates

F39.quote: Because the Generator Product is always the Signer in the C2PA Conformance Program, and is always the entity listed on the C2PA Conforming Products List, it is accountable for the conformance of the Assets with C2PA manifests that it generates
F39.claim: the signer and the listed entity is always the generator product, accountable for the conformance of the assets it generates
F39.lineage: the unit: conforming products on a public list, with trust lists of CAs

F40.quote: Two Assurance Levels are currently in operation, Assurance Level 1 and Assurance Level 2. … Relying Parties are advised to review and understand the implications of receiving Assets signed by C2PA Claim Signing Certificates of a particular Assurance Level.
F40.claim: two assurance levels in operation; relying parties advised to understand what a level implies

F41.quote: The C2PA Content Credentials Specification includes over 300 normative requirements attributed to Generator Products which create C2PA manifests for consumers. The C2PA Conformance Program will eventually require Claim Generators to demonstrate complete conformance to these exacting requirements in order to receive its approval.
F41.claim: the program's own limit: of over 300 normative generator requirements, complete conformance will be required eventually, not yet (likewise over 150 validator requirements)
F41.lineage: stated limit of the program itself: complete conformance is not yet required

F42.quote: The Conformance Program is administered by an independent Administrator who is free from conflicts … of interest.
F42.claim: an independent Administrator, free from conflicts of interest
F42.lineage: governance: the C2PA, its Steering Committee and Conformance Task Force

F43.quote: The C2PA reserves the right to and remove Applicants from the C2PA Trust List and C2PA TSA Trust List, or revoke the conformant status of a Generator Product or Validator Product on the C2PA Conforming Products List.
F43.claim: the C2PA may remove applicants from the trust lists or revoke conformant status (the sentence's 'right to and remove' as printed)
F43.lineage: the unit: conforming products on a public list, with trust lists of CAs

F44.quote: 0.1 2025-06-02 2026-10-09 First version of conformance program, supporting Spec v2.2. 0.2 2026-07-31 Not set Updated conformance program, supporting Spec v2.2 and v2.4.
F44.claim: versions: v0.1 sunrise 2025-06-02, sunset 2026-10-09 (Spec v2.2); v0.2 sunrise 2026-07-31, sunset not set (Spec v2.2 and v2.4)
F44.lineage: origin and versions: June 2025 (v0.1) to v0.2 (31 July 2026)

F45.quote: The C2PA Conformance Program has created a human-readable form of our public trust lists, the Conformance Explorer (https://spec.c2pa.org/conformance-explorer/).
F45.claim: the Explorer is the human-readable form of the public lists
F45.lineage: the Conformance Explorer and the machine-readable lists

F46.quote: C2PA Conformance Program Documents Released v0.2 Upgrade - LinkedIn Jul 31, 2026 — The C2PA has finally released our Conformance Program documents supporting our 0.2 upgrade.
F46.claim: Scott Perry's post: the v0.2 program documents released, 31 July 2026 (snippet only)
F46.lineage: origin and versions: June 2025 (v0.1) to v0.2 (31 July 2026)
F46.checked_against: the card's title/snippet in the registry's cite_list

F47.quote: Provenance, as C2PA defines it, refers to the facts about the history of a piece of digital content (also known as an asset) in a form such as an image, video, audio recording, or document. At the heart of the C2PA specification is the Content Credential, a cryptographically bound structure that records an asset’s provenance.
F47.claim: provenance as C2PA defines it: facts about an asset's history; the Content Credential, a cryptographically bound structure recording it
F47.lineage: what Content Credentials are: signed, tamper-evident provenance bound to the asset

F48.quote: It is important to highlight that Content Credentials do not provide value judgments about whether a given set of provenance data is 'true', but instead merely whether the provenance information is well-formed and free from tampering, valid and trusted (in that the signer of the Content Credential is associated with a known trust list).
F48.claim: the governing limit: Content Credentials judge whether provenance is well-formed, untampered, valid and trusted (signer on a known trust list), not whether it is true
F48.lineage: stated limits: no judgement of truth, no identity or attribution, incomplete chains

F49.quote: Is provenance always complete? No. Provenance is not always complete. It may happen that an asset is modified in a way that the provenance data is not updated.
F49.claim: provenance is not always complete: a non-aware tool can modify an asset without updating it
F49.lineage: stated limits: no judgement of truth, no identity or attribution, incomplete chains

F50.quote: provenance information alone cannot tell you whether the digital content is true, accurate or factual.
F50.claim: provenance alone cannot tell whether content is true, accurate or factual
F50.lineage: stated limits: no judgement of truth, no identity or attribution, incomplete chains

F51.quote: Can the provenance metadata be removed? Yes it can.
F51.claim: the provenance metadata can be removed
F51.lineage: stated limits: no judgement of truth, no identity or attribution, incomplete chains

F52.quote: The C2PA specification does not directly address the topic of human or organizational identity — that is, the identity of specific humans or organizations involved in the production of a digital asset or content.
F52.claim: the specification does not directly address human or organizational identity (extensions may)
F52.lineage: stated limits: no judgement of truth, no identity or attribution, incomplete chains

F53.quote: the ingredient’s provenance cannot be verified in the same way as the provenance data of the asset in which it is contained.
F53.claim: an ingredient's provenance cannot be verified as the containing asset's can
F53.lineage: stated limits: no judgement of truth, no identity or attribution, incomplete chains

F54.quote: Implementers of this standard can have their implementations accredited by the C2PA, which enables users to trust in that implementation. … However, the trust in the contents of a Content Credential is based on the trust relationship between the creator of the Content Credential and the consumer of that Content Credential. This trust relationship is not defined by the C2PA
F54.claim: accreditation gives trust in an implementation; trust in a credential's contents rests on the creator–consumer relationship, which C2PA does not define
F54.lineage: stated limits: no judgement of truth, no identity or attribution, incomplete chains

F55.claim: the list's unit: a record per product (applicant, status, product type, distinguished name, assurance, spec and program versions, dates); 286 records at reading, all 'conformant' (254 generator, 32 validator products; 11 generator products at max level 2)

F56.claim: the first record, Google's Pixel Camera, at max assurance level 2 by Android key attestation

F57.quote: raw wikitext (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=C2PA_Conformance_Program&action=raw&redirect=no, 2026-10-29T17:11:57Z): HTTP 404 (Wikimedia Error page; saved as B11.wiki) rendered page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C2PA_Conformance_Program, 2026-10-29T17:12:33Z): HTTP 404 … Wikipedia does not have an article with this exact name.
F57.claim: Wikipedia has no article 'C2PA Conformance Program'; the program is a section of Content Credentials, and the names C2PA and Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity redirect to a section of Content Authenticity Initiative

F58.locus: Content Authenticity Initiative § Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity ¶1–2
F58.quote: The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) is an open, cross-industry technical standards body established on February 22, 2021.
F58.claim: the operator: an open cross-industry standards body established 22 February 2021 (a project of the Joint Development Foundation, Linux Foundation affiliate)
F58.lineage: governance: the C2PA, its Steering Committee and Conformance Task Force

F59.quote: Experts have also documented ways in which attackers can bypass C2PA’s safeguards, by altering provenance metadata, removing or forging watermarks, and mimicking digital fingerprints. … Besides the fact that C2PA doesn't address the question of whether the content is accurate, another shortcoming is that typical signing tools don't verify the accuracy of the metadata either, so users can't rely on the provenance data either unless they have reason to trust that the signer properly verified it.
F59.claim: criticism: C2PA's safeguards can be bypassed; it does not address accuracy, and signing tools do not verify metadata accuracy
F59.lineage: security: tamper evidence asserted and its demonstrated breaks

F60.quote: In early-to-mid 2024, the C2PA established the Conformance Task Force to transition its open technical specifications into a verifiable compliance model to foster market trust. The task force utilized the Trust over IP (ToIP) Governance Metamodel to structure its compliance policies.
F60.claim: the Task Force established in early-to-mid 2024 to turn the specifications into a verifiable compliance model, structured on the ToIP Governance Metamodel
F60.lineage: origin and versions: June 2025 (v0.1) to v0.2 (31 July 2026)

F61.quote: The C2PA Conformance Program soft-launched on June 4, 2025, at the Content Authenticity Initiative (CAI) Summit, … followed by a full public launch in October 2025. … The transition concluded on December 31, 2025, when the C2PA Interim Trust List was officially deprecated.
F61.claim: soft launch 4 June 2025, full launch October 2025; the Interim Trust List deprecated 31 December 2025
F61.lineage: origin and versions: June 2025 (v0.1) to v0.2 (31 July 2026)

F62.quote: In October 2026, security researcher David Buchanan demonstrated a vulnerability in the C2PA specification that allows an attacker to alter an image without invalidating its cryptographic signatures or trusted timestamps.
F62.claim: October 2026: a demonstrated vulnerability lets an image be altered without invalidating signatures or trusted timestamps (byte-range exclusions)
F62.lineage: security: tamper evidence asserted and its demonstrated breaks

F63.locus: Content Credentials § C2PA Conformance Program › Conforming Implementations ¶1
F63.quote: While the C2PA Conformance Explorer … registry indexes over 200 active products, ecosystem data indicates that 10 organizations have deployed products that simultaneously complete the Conformance Program and achieve on-boarding onto the central C2PA Trust List.
F63.claim: over 200 products on the Explorer, but 10 organizations with deployed products both conforming and on the Trust List

F64.quote: As of mid-2026, major dedicated camera manufacturers (Leica, Nikon, and Canon) do not participate in the official C2PA Conformance Program. … As of 2026, no dedicated camera implementations had achieved compliance under the C2PA Conformance Program.
F64.claim: no dedicated camera implementation conformant as of 2026; Leica, Nikon and Canon outside the program

F65.quote: As of mid-2026, no desktop application had achieved compliance under the C2PA Conformance Program.
F65.claim: no desktop application conformant as of mid-2026

F66.locus: Content Credentials › Mobile apps with Camera Support (Android)
F66.quote: In August 2026, security researcher David Buchanan demonstrated that the C2PA implementation on Android is vulnerable to forgery. … root access allows an attacker to command the system to sign arbitrary data, generating fabricated images with valid authenticity signatures. Google recognized the vulnerability but designated the report as "Won't fix (infeasible)"
F66.claim: August 2026: on Android, root access lets the hardware-held key sign fabricated images with valid signatures; Google: 'Won't fix (infeasible)'
F66.lineage: security: tamper evidence asserted and its demonstrated breaks

F67.locus: Content Credentials § Distinction between provenance and factual accuracy
F67.quote: Content Credentials merely verify provenance and digital integrity without assessing the objective truth of the content itself. Consequently, a fabricated or misleading image can maintain a valid cryptographic credential that confirms its origin while validating deceptive content as technically authentic.
F67.claim: the encyclopedia's distinction: a fabricated image can carry a valid credential
F67.lineage: stated limits: no judgement of truth, no identity or attribution, incomplete chains

It validates that an implementation correctly creates, signs, and reads C2PA manifests, while protecting those manifests and their associated assets through proven cryptographic methods and certificate validation."; F35 (B7, §1 Introduction ¶3): "The Specification has seen wide-scale acceptance but is limited without a robust governance framework and conformance program to provide required transparency for relying parties and accountability for governed parties which need to demonstrate recognized conformance of Specification requirements."; F36 (B7, §2.11 C2PA Conformance Program): "A risk-based governance program intended to hold Applicants who want to demonstrate their conformance to its requirements and then differentiate themselves through C2PA recognition by satisfying program requirements being acknowledged as achieving that level of conformance. translation.lineage: what Content Credentials are: signed, tamper-evident provenance bound to the asset
translation.received: F25 (B6, FAQ: What are Content Credentials? ¶1–2): "Content Credentials provide a cryptographically secure way to capture and express content provenance. … In the context of C2PA, content provenance is captured and preserved using Content Credentials, the technical standard the C2PA produces, providing tamper-evident, cryptographically signed data structures that travel with the asset."; F28 (B6, FAQ: Are Content Credentials a form of DRM? ¶1): "No, Content Credentials are not a form of DRM (Digital Rights Management)."; F47 (B9, Explainer 2.4 §2 ¶2): "Provenance, as C2PA defines it, refers to the facts about the history of a piece of digital content (also known as an asset) in a form such as an image, video, audio recording, or document. At the heart of the C2PA specification is the Content Credential, a cryptographically bound structure that records an asset’s provenance."

translation.lineage: stated limits: no judgement of truth, no identity or attribution, incomplete chains
translation.received: F27 (B6, FAQ: Does validation … ensure that the entire chain of provenance is known, including ingredients? ¶2): "While the primary asset’s Content Credential can validate that the ingredients were checked at the time of use, the full verification of each ingredient’s provenance requires access to its data. Without it, only the presence of prior validation (not the complete ingredient chain) can be confirmed."; F29 (B6, FAQ: What happens if C2PA metadata is stripped …? ¶1): "While C2PA Manifests are typically embedded in the asset, they can be separated. To address this, C2PA supports durable credentials via soft bindings—such as invisible watermarking or fingerprinting—that can help rediscover the associated Content Credential even if it’s removed from the file."; F32 (B6, FAQ: Can organizations or individuals use Content Credentials to achieve attribution of their content? ¶1): "The core C2PA Content Credentials specification does not support attribution of content to individuals or organizations, so that it can remain maximally privacy-preserving."; F48 (B9, Explainer 2.4 §2 ¶3): "It is important to highlight that Content Credentials do not provide value judgments about whether a given set of provenance data is 'true', but instead merely whether the provenance information is well-formed and free from tampering, valid and trusted (in that the signer of the Content Credential is associated with a known trust list)."; F49 (B9, Explainer 2.4 §7.2.1): "Is provenance always complete? No. Provenance is not always complete. It may happen that an asset is modified in a way that the provenance data is not updated."; F50 (B9, Explainer 2.4 §7.2.2): "provenance information alone cannot tell you whether the digital content is true, accurate or factual."; F51 (B9, Explainer 2.4 §7.2.3): "Can the provenance metadata be removed? Yes it can."; F52 (B9, Explainer 2.4 §7.2.4): "The C2PA specification does not directly address the topic of human or organizational identity — that is, the identity of specific humans or organizations involved in the production of a digital asset or content."; F53 (B9, Explainer 2.4 §7.3.2): "the ingredient’s provenance cannot be verified in the same way as the provenance data of the asset in which it is contained."; F54 (B9, Explainer 2.4 §7.5.1): "Implementers of this standard can have their implementations accredited by the C2PA, which enables users to trust in that implementation. … However, the trust in the contents of a Content Credential is based on the trust relationship between the creator of the Content Credential and the consumer of that Content Credential. This trust relationship is not defined by the C2PA"; F67 (B13, Content Credentials § Distinction between provenance and factual accuracy): "Content Credentials merely verify provenance and digital integrity without assessing the objective truth of the content itself. Consequently, a fabricated or misleading image can maintain a valid cryptographic credential that confirms its origin while validating deceptive content as technically authentic."

translation.lineage: security: tamper evidence asserted and its demonstrated breaks
translation.received: F31 (B6, FAQ: How secure is C2PA? ¶1–2): "Any tampering with the asset or its metadata invalidates the cryptographic hash and signature, making alterations immediately detectable. … Faking Content Credentials would require breaking current cryptographic standards—an infeasible task with today’s technology."; F59 (B12, Content Authenticity Initiative § Criticism ¶2–3): "Experts have also documented ways in which attackers can bypass C2PA’s safeguards, by altering provenance metadata, removing or forging watermarks, and mimicking digital fingerprints. … Besides the fact that C2PA doesn't address the question of whether the content is accurate, another shortcoming is that typical signing tools don't verify the accuracy of the metadata either, so users can't rely on the provenance data either unless they have reason to trust that the signer properly verified it."; F62 (B13, Content Credentials § C2PA Conformance Program ¶3): "In October 2026, security researcher David Buchanan demonstrated a vulnerability in the C2PA specification that allows an attacker to alter an image without invalidating its cryptographic signatures or trusted timestamps."; F66 (B13, Content Credentials › Mobile apps with Camera Support (Android)): "In August 2026, security researcher David Buchanan demonstrated that the C2PA implementation on Android is vulnerable to forgery. … root access allows an attacker to command the system to sign arbitrary data, generating fabricated images with valid authenticity signatures.
